theory_title: Why your money shrinks while it sits
theory_content: Inflation is the rate at which prices rise, and in India it has averaged about 6% a year. That means ₹1,00,000 kept in a drawer buys roughly ₹94,000 worth of goods a year later, and about half as much after twelve years. This is why "keeping money safe" and "keeping money whole" are different problems. Any return below the inflation rate is a loss you cannot see on the statement.

A real return is what is left after inflation. A fixed deposit paying 6.8% during 6% inflation earns a real return of about 0.8% — and after tax at a 30% slab, the nominal 6.8% becomes 4.8%, which is a real loss of 1.2% a year. Whenever someone quotes a return, ask what it is after inflation and after tax. Those two subtractions change almost every comparison.

theory_title: Every rupee is a choice about another rupee
theory_content: Spending ₹95,000 on a phone is not only ₹95,000. Invested at 12% for twenty years, that amount becomes about ₹9,16,000. That figure is the opportunity cost — what the money would have become if left alone. This is not an argument against spending; it is an argument for knowing the second number before you decide.

theory_title: One number that describes your position
theory_content: Net worth is everything you own minus everything you owe. A person with a ₹60 lakh flat and a ₹55 lakh home loan has a net worth of ₹5 lakh from that asset, not ₹60 lakh. Tracking it once a quarter is the single most useful habit in personal finance, because income tells you about a month and net worth tells you about a decade.
